decisions_log.decision: D9 consequence (a) corrected rather than transcribed
options_considered: append with (a) corrected and the correction explained
decisions_log.why: D9 as drafted says v3 was withdrawn before execution and no v3 artifacts exist. v3 ran to completion, its gate and its Arm A test both passed, and Cooper rejected it on row 0; artifacts are committed. A decision record must not contradict the repo, and both surviving v3 results are load-bearing for D9's own argument.
A zero interval cannot exist under it by construction, so the log transform needs no imputed value. resolution_floor runs alongside; row 5 measured the difference at exactly 0.0000.

decisions_log.chose: moving median, evaluated at anchors spaced window/10 apart and interpolated
decisions_log.why: The log-interval sequence is heavy-tailed with long quiet stretches; a moving mean is dragged by them. The anchored evaluation is O(10n) instead of O(n log w) for windows of ~1e5 samples, and the anchor spacing is a tenth of a window so the interpolated location cannot move more than the median does across a tenth of a window.

options_considered: kernel-smooth the histogram before peak finding
decisions_log.chose: none; peak prominence does the work
decisions_log.why: Smoothing would reintroduce a bandwidth -- the exact free parameter D9 exists to remove.

surprises: SHARED ROOT CAUSE across all five method families: every method needed a reference level or a resolution -- a constant rate, a flanking baseline, a smoothing bandwidth, an envelope scale, a normalization window -- and in every case the answer tracked that choice rather than the market. Arm A's burst count correlated +0.96 with print count; v4's +0.87 with a log-log slope of 0.92, above Arm A's own 0.85. v3 was the sole exception on that test (+0.28) and was rejected on the tape instead. The binary question 'are there bursts?' is ill-posed without constraining how fast the underlying rate may vary, which is what Phase 10b re-poses as a timescale question.

Row 1 fails at Spearman 0.8748 and log-log slope 0.9224 -- the slope is ABOVE Arm A's own 0.85. Five methods have now been tried and this is the second-worst result on the test that matters, after Arm A itself.

The mechanism is visible in chart 01 and is not the one D9 anticipated. Every threshold-bearing event has an isolated narrow spike at a normalized log interval of about -3.5, separated from the broad main body by a deep trough. The void gate finds that trough and takes it. The spike is order fragmentation -- one marketable order sweeping several resting orders produces several prints microseconds apart -- so the method separates multi-fill microstructure from everything else, not bursts from quiet. Multi-fill count scales with print count, hence 0.87.
Median sub-burst duration is 349 nanoseconds against an 80.5 ns timestamp resolution. The decomposition is operating at the resolution of the clock, not the timescale of the tape.

The void gate itself performed well and did the honest thing: it declined on 10/100 events rather than inventing sub-bursts, and the no_threshold events are exactly those whose histograms are smooth and broad with no multi-fill spike. D9's Zaliapin prediction was borne out, just not at the magnitude that would have fired row 2.
Rows 4 and 5 passing is not reassuring in context: a method can be perfectly stable under its own parameters while stably measuring the wrong object, which is what appears to have happened.

The normalization-window sensitivity is 0.1984 -- inside our 0.20 bar but 66x the 0.003 that Ko et al. report for the same 10-30% grid on spike trains. Market tick data does not sit in the published regime.

The causal audit found exactly 2 causal fields out of 18: the D7 detection anchor and the segment derived from it. Everything the phase actually measures is non-causal, and the threshold -- the trough of the completed session's histogram -- is the most non-causal quantity of all.
